meta_description: Essential health and medication guide for traveling in Japan. Covers emergency numbers, pharmacy access, medication restrictions, vaccinations, water safety, and travel insurance tips.

quick_facts.healthcare_type: Universal public insurance (residents) / Pay-out-of-pocket for tourists
quick_facts.water: Safe — tap water is potable nationwide
quick_facts.pharmacy_access: Good — drugstores (Drug Sekai, Matsumoto Kiyoshi) widely available

healthcare_overview_html:
🏥 Healthcare Overview

Japan has one of the world's best healthcare systems for residents, with universal coverage and consistently high quality. For tourists, however, the system works differently: you'll pay out-of-pocket at point of service, and costs can add up fast.

Medical facilities in Japan are modern, clean, and staffed by well-trained professionals. English-speaking doctors exist but are not guaranteed outside major cities like Tokyo, Osaka, and Kyoto. Consider carrying a Japanese-language hospital introduction card or using the Japan National Tourist Organization (JNTO) hotline: 050-3816-2787 (English, 24/7).

💡 Good to know

Japan does not have a reciprocal healthcare agreement with most countries. Your home-country health plan likely won't cover you here. Travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is strongly recommended.

Hospital Quality

Major urban hospitals (especially in Tokyo) are world-class and some have dedicated International Departments. Rural hospitals may have limited English and fewer specialists. For anything serious, get to a large city hospital.

📋 What to bring

Passport, travel insurance documents, list of current medications (in Japanese if possible), and any relevant medical records.
pharmacy_guide_html:
💊 Pharmacy Guide

Japan separates medications more strictly than many Western countries. Most antibiotics, prescription-strength painkillers, and other common drugs cannot be purchased OTC — you need a doctor's prescription (shouhosen 処方箋).

What's Available OTC

  • Basic pain relievers: acetaminophen/paracetamol (タイレノール), ibuprofen
  • Cold & flu medications (but formulations differ from the US/EU)
  • Allergy medication: antihistamines
  • Digestive aids: antacids, loperamide (Imodium equivalent)
  • Topical antibiotics and antiseptic ointments
  • Band-aids, basic wound care

⚠️ PSE drugs

Medications containing pseudoephedrine (some cold medicines) are restricted in Japan. Declare any such medications at customs and carry a prescription.

Major Pharmacy Chains

  • Drug Sekai (ドラッグスクリーン) — large, English-friendly, Axia brand
  • Matsumoto Kiyoshi (マツモトキヨシ) — ubiquitous in cities
  • Don Quijote (ドン・キホーテ) — 24h, huge range, some English labels
  • Kokumin (국은) — nationwide chain

Hours & Tips

  • Most pharmacies: 9am–9pm
  • 24-hour pharmacies exist in major cities (check Google Maps)
  • Bring a photo of your medication (original packaging helps too)
  • Pharmacists in Japan are helpful but may not speak English — translation apps help

💡 Tip

For prescription refills while traveling, visit a clinic first (expect ¥5,000–¥15,000 for the consultation). Ask the doctor to write the prescription in English and Japanese.
medications_html:
💉 Medications & Restrictions

Japan has strict drug laws. What's legal over-the-counter in your home country may be controlled or prohibited in Japan. This is taken very seriously — penalties can include arrest and deportation.

Bringing Medication Into Japan

You can bring a 90-day personal supply of prescription medication for your own use, but you must:

  • Carry it in the original labeled container
  • Have a copy of your prescription (English + Japanese translation recommended)
  • Declare it at customs
  • For controlled substances (see below), complete the Yakkan Shoumei (入境確認証) advance import notification from the Pharmaceutical Affairs Agency

Controlled / Restricted Substances

🚫 Commonly problematic for travelers

  • Adderall / amphetamine-based ADHD meds (requires advance approval)
  • Codeine-containing products (legal limits are very low)
  • Sleep aids containing flunitrazepam (Rohypnol) — prohibited
  • Tramadol — controlled substance
  • Some strong painkiller formulations

Common Traveler Meds Availability

✅ Easily found

  • Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
  • Ibuprofen (Advil)
  • Loratadine (Claritin)
  • Omeprazole (acid reflux)
  • Oral rehydration salts

⚠️ Requires prescription

  • Antibiotics
  • Insulin
  • Albuterol inhalers
  • Epinephrine auto-injectors (EpiPen)
  • Stronger antihistamines

⚠️ Important

If you take a controlled or psychiatric medication, contact the Japan Embassy or consulate before traveling to confirm the import process. The Yokkan Shoumei form must be submitted at least 6 weeks before travel.
insurance_html:
🛡️ Travel Insurance

Travel insurance is strongly recommended for Japan — not legally required, but the cost of medical care as a foreign tourist can be significant. A hospital stay in Japan can run ¥50,000–¥500,000+ per night, and air ambulance evacuation out of Japan can cost $20,000–$100,000+.

Coverage to Look For

  • Medical coverage: minimum ¥3,000,000 (~$20,000 USD)
  • Medical evacuation & repatriation: essential — Japan's islands may require helicopter evacuation in emergencies
  • Trip cancellation / interruption: useful for typhoon season (Jun–Oct)
  • Personal liability: recommended for a busy travel itinerary

Average Cost

A comprehensive Japan policy typically costs $3–$8 per day per person. Annual multi-trip policies run $100–$300. Popular providers for Japan travel: World Nomads, SafetyWing, Allianz, Seven Corners.

💡 Pro tip

Check if your credit card includes travel insurance — many premium cards (Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum) include medical evacuation coverage. Verify the limits and exclusions before relying on it.

Schengen / Visa Note

Japan does not require travel insurance for visa-free entry from most countries (US, EU, UK, AU, CA, etc. — typically 90 days or less). However, if you're applying for a longer-stay visa, proof of insurance may be required.
vaccinations_html:
💉 Vaccinations

No vaccinations are required for entry to Japan from the US, EU, UK, Canada, Australia, or most countries (unless arriving from a yellow fever risk zone, which requires proof of YF vaccine).

Recommended Vaccinations

📋 Routine immunizations — keep current

MMR, DTaP, influenza, varicella, COVID-19 — the standard shots you'd have at home.

  • Hepatitis A: recommended for most travelers (food/water exposure)
  • Hepatitis B: recommended for stays >6 months or expected medical procedures
  • Japanese Encephalitis: consider if spending >1 month in rural areas during summer (Jun–Oct)
  • Rabies: not typically recommended for tourists; relevant for extended rural stays or animal workers
  • Tick-borne encephalitis: not endemic in Japan

Where to Get Travel Vaccinations

  • Travel clinics: Passport Health, iTravel, local public health departments
  • Your GP / primary care doctor
  • University health centers for students

💡 Timing

Most travel vaccinations should be completed 4–6 weeks before departure. Some require multiple doses over several months.
food_water_html:
🚰 Water & Food Safety

✅ Tap water is safe to drink everywhere in Japan. Tap water is potable in all 47 prefectures — this has been the case since the 1990s. Bottled water is available everywhere if you prefer it (¥100–¥200 per bottle).

Bottled vs. Tap

In Tokyo and other major cities, tap water is actually higher quality than many bottled waters. The only caveat: some older buildings may have rusty pipes. If a building looks very old, drinking from the tap in your room may have a slight taste issue — still safe, just not pleasant.

💧 Ice is safe

Ice in drinks is made from treated tap water and is safe to consume throughout Japan.

Food Safety

Japan has excellent food safety standards. Restaurant hygiene is generally very high, and food poisoning incidents are rare compared to many other destinations. That said:

  • Raw egg (tamago kake gohan) is safe — Japan's eggs are pasteurized and rated for raw consumption
  • sashimi and raw seafood from reputable restaurants is safe
  • Watch out for Fukusuri (botulism from improperly prepared home-pickled vegetables) — very rare but known in rural areas
  • Temperatures in summer (Jul–Aug) can reach 35°C+ — keep perishable items brief

🍣 General rule

If it looks fresh, it probably is. Japan's food culture demands freshness. Convenience store (7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart) food is also surprisingly safe and high quality — a great backup.
emergency_contacts_html:
🚨 Emergency Contacts

⚠️ Medical Emergency

🆘 Call 119 — for ambulance and fire. Say "Kyūkyū desu" (救急です = "It's an emergency") and stay on the line. Ambulances are free in Japan, but treatment at the hospital is not.

Key Emergency Numbers

  • 🆘 119 — Ambulance / Fire (medical emergencies)
  • 🚔 110 — Police (non-medical emergencies, crime)
  • ⚓ 118 — Maritime rescue

Tourist Support Hotlines

  • JNTO Medical Hotline (English, 24/7): 050-3816-2787 — staffed by nurses, can help find English-speaking hospitals
  • Japan Visitor Hotline (Japan Tourism Agency): 050-3816-2787 (same number)
  • COVID-19 Hotline: 0120-565-653 (Ministry of Health)

US Embassy (for US citizens)

  • Address: 1-10-5 Akasaka, Minato-ku, Tokyo 107-8420
  • Phone: +81-3-3224-5000
  • Website: jp.usembassy.gov
  • Note: Embassies can assist with replacement of lost passports and notification of family, but cannot pay for medical care.

⚠️ Other nationalities

Check your country's embassy or consulate page for emergency contact information. Most major embassies are in Tokyo. Japan has no 911 equivalent — 119 is for medical/fire emergencies only.
